concepts.name: Multiplying by 5, 25, 50 and 125
concepts.description: 5 = 10 ÷ 2, 25 = 100 ÷ 4, 50 = 100 ÷ 2 and 125 = 1000 ÷ 8: multiply by the power of 10 and divide by the small number, whichever order keeps the numbers whole.

concepts.name: Multiplying by 111, 99 and 999
concepts.description: Multiplying by 111 adds digits in a sliding window of three. Multiplying by 99 or 999 is multiplying by 100 or 1000 and taking the number away once.

concepts.name: The base method
concepts.description: For two numbers near the same base (10, 100, 1000): left part = one number plus the other’s surplus, right part = product of the two surpluses (or deficits), written with as many digits as the base has zeros.

concepts.name: Cross multiplication
concepts.description: For ab × cd: units = b × d, tens = a × d + b × c, hundreds = a × c, carrying leftwards. One line of working, no partial products.

concepts.name: Percentages as fractions in a calculation
concepts.description: Swap a percentage for its fraction (37.5% = 3/8, 16⅔% = 1/6) so that multiplying becomes one division. And x% of y always equals y% of x.

concepts.name: Checking with digit sums
concepts.description: Casting out nines: the digital root of a product equals the product of the digital roots (reduced). A mismatch proves an answer wrong; a match does not prove it right.

concepts.name: Quick division
concepts.description: Dividing by 5, 25 or 125 is multiplying by 2, 4 or 8 and shifting the decimal point. A composite divisor can be taken in stages: ÷ 36 is ÷ 4 then ÷ 9.

formulas.title: Multiplying by 5, 25 and 125
formulas.prompt: What is the quick way to multiply by 5, 25 or 125?
formulas.explanation: 5, 25 and 125 are 10, 100 and 1000 cut into 2, 4 and 8 equal parts. Halving, quartering or eighthing is easier than multiplying.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing by the wrong number: × 25 is ÷ 4, not ÷ 5.

formulas.title: Multiplying by 111
formulas.prompt: How do you multiply a two- or three-digit number by 111 in one line?
formulas.formula:
abc × 111 = a | a+b | a+b+c | b+c | c (carry when a sum passes 9)
ab × 111 = a | a+b | a+b | b
formulas.explanation: 111 = 100 + 10 + 1, so each digit is added to the place, the place above and the place two above. Reading the sums in a window of three gives every column.
formulas.commonMistake: Using a window of two (the × 11 rule) for 111.

formulas.title: Multiplying by 99 and 999
formulas.prompt: What is the quick way to multiply by 99 or 999?
formulas.explanation: 99 is one short of 100, so the product is one n short of n hundreds.

formulas.title: Base method (Nikhilam)
formulas.prompt: How do you multiply two numbers that are both close to 100?
formulas.formula:
x × y = (x + (y − B)) | (x − B)(y − B)
Right part has as many digits as B has zeros; carry any excess
formulas.explanation: x × y = B(x + y − B) + (x − B)(y − B), which is algebra, not magic. Cross-subtracting a deficit (or adding a surplus) gives the left part; the product of the two deficits gives the right part.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to carry when the right part has too many digits: 88 × 87 has right part 12 × 13 = 156, so 75 | 156 becomes 7,656.

formulas.title: One number above the base, one below
formulas.prompt: One number is above the base and the other below. How does the base method change?
formulas.formula:
Right part = surplus × (−deficit), which is negative
Borrow 1 from the left part (worth one base) to clear it
formulas.explanation: The method is unchanged; only the sign of the right part is. A left part of 101 and right part −12 means 101 × 100 − 12.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing 101 | 12 and ignoring the minus sign (10,112).

formulas.title: Cross multiplication
formulas.prompt: How do you multiply two two-digit numbers in a single line?
formulas.formula:
ab × cd = a×c | a×d + b×c | b×d
Work from the right, carrying leftwards
formulas.explanation: (10a + b)(10c + d) = 100ac + 10(ad + bc) + bd. The three columns are just those three groups.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to add the carry into the next column.

formulas.title: Percentages to swap for fractions
formulas.prompt: Which percentages should you replace by fractions before calculating?
formulas.explanation: Each one turns a percentage of a number into one division and maybe one multiplication. Bank papers choose numbers that divide exactly.

formulas.title: Swap the percentage and the number
formulas.prompt: x% of y looks awkward. What simple swap might make it easy?
formulas.formula: x% of y = y% of x
formulas.explanation: Both equal xy ÷ 100. Use whichever way round has a friendly percentage.
formulas.commonMistake: Swapping only one of the two numbers.

formulas.title: Casting out nines
formulas.prompt: How can you check a multiplication in a few seconds without redoing it?
formulas.formula:
Digital root of (a × b) = digital root of (dr(a) × dr(b))
Mismatch → the answer is wrong
formulas.explanation: A number leaves the same remainder on division by 9 as its digit sum, and remainders multiply. The same check works for addition and subtraction.
formulas.commonMistake: Trusting a match completely: swapped digits (4,402) pass the check too.

formulas.title: Dividing by 5, 25 and 125
formulas.prompt: What is the quick way to divide by 5, 25 or 125?
formulas.explanation: Dividing by 25 is dividing by 100 and multiplying by 4, since 100 ÷ 25 = 4. Moving a decimal point is free.
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying by 4 but forgetting to divide by 100.

formulas.title: Divide in stages
formulas.prompt: How do you divide by a composite number such as 36 or 48 without long division?
formulas.formula:
÷ (p × q) = ÷ p, then ÷ q
Choose factors with easy tests: 4, 8, 9, 6
formulas.explanation: Dividing by a product is dividing by each factor in turn. Small divisors are easy to do mentally, and their divisibility tests tell you early whether the answer is whole.
formulas.commonMistake: Splitting 36 into 6 × 6 and dividing by 6 only once.

levels.title: Shortcuts That Are Really Algebra
levels.description: Friendly multipliers, multiplying by 111 and 99, and the base method, each with the reason it works.

blocks.title: Friendly multipliers
blocks.body: 25 is 100 ÷ 4, so 864 × 25 is 86,400 ÷ 4. 125 is 1,000 ÷ 8 and 5 is 10 ÷ 2. Exam numbers are usually chosen so that these divisions come out exact.

blocks.title: Near a base: work with the gaps
blocks.body:
97 and 96 are 3 and 4 below 100. Take one gap from the other number: 97 − 4 = 93. Multiply the gaps: 3 × 4 = 12. Together, 97 × 96 = 9,312.

Above 100 the gaps are added: 103 × 104 → 103 + 4 = 107 | 3 × 4 = 12 → 10,712.

blocks.title: Why it works
blocks.caption: a and b are the gaps below 100. Cutting both strips from 100 × 100 removes the a × b corner twice, so it is added back.

blocks.body: Multiplying by 99 is multiplying by 100 and taking the number away once: 47 × 99 = 4,700 − 47 = 4,653. The Simplification topic has the × 11 rule and squares ending in 5.

levels.title: Speed Maths Methods
levels.description: Friendly multipliers, × 111, the base method, cross multiplication and percentage–fraction swaps.

levels.title: One-Line Calculations
levels.description: Each method once, with friendly numbers.

levels.title: Above, Below and Across
levels.description: Numbers above the base, mixed bases, cross multiplication with carries and × 99.

levels.title: Carries, Bigger Bases and Shares
levels.description: Right parts that overflow, base 1,000, percentage chains and a faulty working to fix.

levels.title: Advanced: Checking and Dividing Fast
levels.description: Catch wrong answers with digit sums, and divide by 25, 125 or a composite number without long division.

blocks.title: Casting out nines
blocks.body:
Reduce each number to one digit by adding its digits again and again: 86 → 14 → 5 and 47 → 11 → 2. For a product, multiply the two: 5 × 2 = 10 → 1. If the answer’s digits do not also reduce to 1, the answer is wrong.

86 × 47 = 4,042 → 10 → 1, so it passes.
Passing proves nothing about swapped digits or a misplaced zero: 4,402 and 40,420 pass as well. The check catches most slips, not all.

blocks.title: Division by friendly numbers
blocks.body: ÷ 25 is × 4 ÷ 100: 3,450 ÷ 25 = 13,800 ÷ 100 = 138. ÷ 125 is × 8 ÷ 1,000. For a divisor such as 36, divide by 4 and then by 9.

levels.title: Challenge: Beat the Clock
levels.description: Timed checks, divisions and multiplications: about 45 seconds each.

questions.question: Find 864 × 25 without long multiplication.

hints.text: 25 is a quarter of 100.
Divide 864 by 4 first; it divides exactly.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 5 instead of 4.

questions.question: What is 52 × 111?
questions.explanation: For a two-digit number ab, ab × 111 = a | a + b | a + b | b. Here 5 | 7 | 7 | 2 = 5,772.
questions.method: Sliding window of digit sums.
commonMistakes: Using the × 11 pattern (572).

questions.question: Use the base method to find 98 × 94.
questions.explanation: Deficits from 100 are 2 and 6. Left part: 98 − 6 = 92 (or 94 − 2). Right part: 2 × 6 = 12. So 98 × 94 = 9,212.
questions.method: Cross-subtract, multiply the deficits.

hints.text: How far below 100 is each number?
Take one deficit from the other number; multiply the deficits.

commonMistakes: Adding the deficits to get the left part (100 + 8).

questions.question: What is 37.5% of 1,840?
questions.method: Replace the percentage by its fraction.

hints.text: 37.5% is three times 12.5%.

questions.question: Put the steps of 32 × 41 by cross multiplication in order.
questions.explanation: Cross multiplication works from the right: units first, then the cross products for tens, then the leading digits, carrying each time. 32 × 41 = 1,312.
questions.method: Right to left: units, crosswise, leading digits.

hints.text: Carries move to the left, so start at the right.
The crosswise step is the middle one.

commonMistakes: Starting with the hundreds and having nowhere to put the carries.

questions.question: Find 107 × 112 by the base method.
questions.explanation: Surpluses over 100 are 7 and 12. Left part: 107 + 12 = 119. Right part: 7 × 12 = 84. So 107 × 112 = 11,984.
questions.method: Above the base, cross-add.

hints.text: Both numbers are above 100, so add the surplus.
Right part: 7 × 12.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the surplus as if the numbers were below 100.

questions.question: What is 106 × 94?
questions.explanation: Surplus 6 and deficit 6. Left part: 106 − 6 = 100. Right part: 6 × (−6) = −36. 100 | −36 means 10,000 − 36 = 9,964. (Also 100² − 6² = 9,964.)
questions.method: Mixed base: negative right part, borrow.

hints.text: One number is above 100 and one below, so the right part is negative.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the sign and answering 10,036.

questions.question: Find 67 × 48 by cross multiplication.
questions.explanation: Units: 7 × 8 = 56 → 6, carry 5. Tens: 6 × 8 + 7 × 4 = 76, plus 5 = 81 → 1, carry 8. Hundreds: 6 × 4 = 24, plus 8 = 32. Answer 3,216.
questions.method: Vertically and crosswise.

hints.text: Units digit first: 7 × 8.
Tens: 6 × 8 + 7 × 4, then add the carry.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to add a carry into the next column.
Using only 6 × 8 for the tens and missing the cross product 7 × 4.

questions.question: What is 16⅔% of 4,326?
questions.method: Percentage → fraction → one division.

hints.text: 16⅔% is one-sixth.
Divide 4,326 by 6.

commonMistakes: Treating 16⅔% as 1/16.

questions.question: What is 7,346 × 99?
questions.method: × 100, then take one copy away.

hints.text: Work out 7,34,600 − 7,346 carefully.

commonMistakes: Subtracting 99 or 1 instead of 7,346.

questions.question: Multiplying a number by 125 gives the same result as multiplying it by 1,000 and then dividing by 8.
questions.method: Write the multiplier as a power of 10 divided by something small.

hints.text: What is 1,000 ÷ 8?

commonMistakes: Confusing it with × 25 (÷ 4) and saying false.

questions.question: Find 988 × 997 using the base 1,000.
questions.explanation: Deficits from 1,000 are 12 and 3. Left part: 988 − 3 = 985. Right part: 12 × 3 = 36, written as three digits: 036. Answer 9,85,036.
questions.method: Base 1,000: three-digit right part.

hints.text: With base 1,000 the right part must have three digits.
Left part: 988 − 3.

commonMistakes: Writing 36 with two digits (98,536).

questions.question: What is 88 × 87?
questions.explanation: Deficits 12 and 13. Left part 88 − 13 = 75. Right part 12 × 13 = 156, which has three digits: keep 56 and carry 1 into the left part. 76 | 56 = 7,656.
questions.method: Base method with a carry from the right part.

hints.text: The right part 12 × 13 has three digits, but base 100 allows only two.
Carry the hundreds digit of 156 into the left part.

commonMistakes: Writing 75 | 156 = 75,156 without carrying.

questions.question: A prize of ₹2,880 is shared. Asha gets 62.5% of it, Ravi gets 11 1/9% of what is left, and Kiran gets the rest. How much does Kiran get?
questions.method: Turn each percentage into a fraction of the right base.

hints.text: Ravi’s share is taken of what is left after Asha, not of ₹2,880.

commonMistakes: Taking Ravi’s 1/9 of the whole ₹2,880.

questions.question: In which step does this working first go wrong?
questions.context:
Find 76 × 58 by cross multiplication.

Step 1: Units: 6 × 8 = 48; write 8, carry 4.
Step 2: Tens: 7 × 8 + 6 × 5 = 86; write 6, carry 8.
Step 3: Hundreds: 7 × 5 = 35; 35 + 8 = 43.
Answer: 4,368

options.text: Step 2: the carried 4 was not added to 86

questions.explanation: The tens column must include the carry: 86 + 4 = 90, so write 0 and carry 9. Then the hundreds are 35 + 9 = 44 and the answer is 4,408.
questions.method: Every column adds the carry from the column to its right.

hints.text: Check where the carry from Step 1 went.
Does Step 2 use the 4 carried from the units?

commonMistakes: Blaming Step 3, which only inherits the earlier slip.

questions.question: A student writes 4,738 × 26 = 1,23,198. What does the nines check show?

options.text: It is wrong: the digit sums give 5 for the product but 6 for the answer
It passes, so it must be right
The check cannot be used on products
It is wrong because the answer should be odd

questions.explanation: 4,738 → 22 → 4 and 26 → 8; 4 × 8 = 32 → 5. The answer 1,23,198 → 24 → 6. Since 5 ≠ 6 the answer is certainly wrong (the true product is 1,23,188).
questions.method: Compare digital roots on both sides.

hints.text: Reduce each number to a single digit by adding its digits.
Multiply the two digital roots and reduce again.

commonMistakes: Thinking an even × even answer must be checked by parity alone.

questions.question: Select ALL the results that FAIL the nines check (and so must be wrong).
questions.explanation: (b) 5 × 2 = 10 → 1, but 1,962 → 9: fails. (d) 3 × 2 = 6, but 4,361 → 5: fails. (a) and (e) pass and are right. (c) passes (8 × 1 = 8 and 4,652 → 8) yet is wrong: the true product is 4,625. Swapped digits slip through the check.
questions.method: Digital roots of both sides.

hints.text: Only answers whose digital roots disagree fail the check.
One option is wrong but still passes. Which?

commonMistakes: Selecting (c): it is wrong, but it does not fail the check.

questions.question: Find 4,275 ÷ 25.

hints.text: How many 25s make 100?
Multiply by 4 and move the decimal point two places.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 4 instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Find 13,248 ÷ 48 by dividing in stages.
questions.method: Split the divisor into easy factors.

hints.text: Write 48 as a product of two small numbers.
Divide by 8 first; then by 6.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 8 and by 4 (that is ÷ 32).

questions.question: What is 2,345 ÷ 125?

hints.text: How many 125s make 1,000?
Multiply by 8, then move the decimal point three places.

commonMistakes: Moving the decimal point two places (187.6) or four (1.876).

questions.question: What should the next step be?
questions.context:
You worked out 8,465 × 37 = 3,13,205 and want to check it with digit sums.

Step 1: 8,465 → 8 + 4 + 6 + 5 = 23 → 5
Step 2: 37 → 3 + 7 = 10 → 1

options.text: Multiply 5 × 1 = 5 and compare it with the digit sum of 3,13,205
Add 5 + 1 = 6 and compare it with the digit sum of 3,13,205
Divide 3,13,205 by 37 to finish the check
Compare 5 with the last digit of 3,13,205

questions.explanation: For a product, multiply the digital roots: 5 × 1 = 5. The answer 3,13,205 → 14 → 5 matches, so the result passes the check.
questions.method: Multiply digital roots for a product, add them for a sum.

hints.text: The original sum was a multiplication, so what do you do with 5 and 1?
Then reduce 3,13,205 to one digit.

commonMistakes: Adding the digital roots, which checks a sum, not a product.

questions.question: Find 48 × 125 + 52 × 125.
questions.method: Factor out the common multiplier first.

hints.text: Both terms are multiples of 125.
What do 48 and 52 add up to?

commonMistakes: Working out each product separately and slipping in the addition.
